question: An IAM user has an identity-based policy that allows s3:* on all resources. The user is also a member of an IAM group whose policy explicitly denies s3:DeleteObject on the bucket named audit-logs. What happens when the user tries to delete an object from audit-logs?
options: The request is allowed, because a policy attached directly to the user takes precedence over group policies.
The request is allowed, because the broader s3:* wildcard overrides more specific deny statements.
The request is denied only if the user signed in without MFA, because explicit denies apply only to sessions without MFA.
The request is denied, because an explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides any allow.
explanation: IAM evaluates all applicable policies together: by default everything is implicitly denied, an allow can override that default, but an explicit deny always wins. It does not matter whether the deny comes from a user, group, or other policy. Wildcards do not override denies, and explicit denies apply regardless of MFA unless a condition says otherwise.

question: A member account in AWS Organizations has a single SCP attached that allows only ec2:*, s3:*, and cloudwatch:* actions; the default FullAWSAccess policy has been removed. An IAM role in the account has the AdministratorAccess managed policy. What happens when the role tries to create an Amazon DynamoDB table?
options: The request is allowed, because the AdministratorAccess managed policy grants every action and SCPs filter only customer managed policies.
The request is denied, because SCPs define the maximum available permissions and the SCP does not allow DynamoDB actions.
The request is allowed, because SCPs restrict IAM users in member accounts but not IAM roles.
The request is denied, because SCPs grant permissions only to the root user of each member account.
explanation: An SCP acts as a permission guardrail: an action must be allowed by both the SCPs in the account's path and the identity's IAM policies. Because this allow-list SCP does not include DynamoDB, the action is denied even with AdministratorAccess. SCPs apply to all users and roles in member accounts, including the root user, and they never grant permissions on their own.

question: A company must prevent all member accounts in its organization from creating resources in any Region other than eu-central-1 and eu-west-1. Global services such as IAM, Amazon CloudFront, and Amazon Route 53 must continue to work. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Attach an IAM policy to every user and role in every member account that allows actions only when aws:RequestedRegion matches one of the two approved Regions.
Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies all actions except a NotAction list of global services when aws:RequestedRegion is not one of the two approved Regions.
Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies all actions whenever aws:RequestedRegion is not eu-central-1 or eu-west-1, applied uniformly with no service exceptions.
Disable every Region other than eu-central-1 and eu-west-1 on the Account settings page of each member account so that API calls to those Regions fail.
explanation: A single SCP with a Region condition enforces the restriction across all member accounts, and exempting global services with NotAction keeps them working because their requests are made to a fixed Region such as us-east-1. IAM policies in every account are hard to maintain and can be changed by account administrators. Denying everything without exceptions breaks global services, and Regions that are enabled by default cannot be disabled.

question: A developer's IAM role has an identity-based policy that allows s3:* and dynamodb:*. The role also has a permissions boundary that allows s3:* and sqs:*. No other policies apply. Which actions can the developer perform?
options: Only Amazon S3 actions
Amazon S3, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon SQS actions
Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB actions
Amazon S3 and Amazon SQS actions
explanation: A permissions boundary sets the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant, so the effective permissions are the intersection of the two. Only S3 is allowed by both. DynamoDB is outside the boundary, and SQS is in the boundary but not granted by the identity policy, and a boundary never grants permissions by itself.

question: A company wants to let application team leads create IAM roles for their own AWS Lambda functions without opening a ticket. The team leads must not be able to create roles with more permissions than a set of approved services allows, and they must not be able to escalate their own privileges. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Grant the team leads the AdministratorAccess managed policy and use an Amazon EventBridge rule on CloudTrail events to alert the security team about every new role.
Attach an SCP to the account that denies iam:CreateRole for every principal except a central platform team, which creates the approved roles on request.
Allow iam:CreateRole only when the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key equals an approved boundary policy, and deny actions that remove or change that boundary.
Allow iam:CreateRole and iam:PassRole without conditions and rely on the Lambda service-linked role to cap the permissions of each function's execution role.
explanation: Requiring a specific permissions boundary on every role the team leads create caps those roles at the approved permissions, and denying changes to boundaries prevents them from removing the cap. AdministratorAccess with after-the-fact review does not prevent escalation. Denying iam:CreateRole blocks the self-service requirement, and Lambda functions use execution roles that the team leads would define, not a service-linked role.

question: A company requires that IAM users can stop or terminate production Amazon EC2 instances only if they authenticated with multi-factor authentication (MFA) during their current session. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Enable a hardware MFA device on the account root user and require engineers to sign in as the root user whenever they stop or terminate production instances.
Enable termination protection on each production instance and associate a virtual MFA device with it so that stop and terminate requests prompt for a code.
Add a condition requiring aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent to be true to the policy statement that allows ec2:StopInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances.
Add an aws:SourceIp condition to the statement that allows ec2:StopInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances so they work only from the corporate VPN range.
explanation: The aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition key is true only when the request uses credentials from an MFA-authenticated session, so the allow applies only in that case. Using the root user for routine work violates best practice. Termination protection has no MFA setting and does not cover stopping instances, and a source IP condition restricts location rather than requiring MFA.

question: An application that runs under an IAM role in account A must read objects from an S3 bucket in account B. The bucket uses SSE-S3 encryption and ACLs are disabled. Which configurations are required? (Select TWO.)
options: An AWS RAM resource share in account B that shares the bucket with account A so that the role can read its objects
An identity-based policy on the role in account A that allows s3:GetObject on the bucket's objects
A bucket policy in account B that allows the account A role to perform s3:GetObject on the bucket's objects
An SCP attached to account B that allows the account A role to perform s3:GetObject on the bucket's objects
A trust policy on the bucket in account B that allows sts:AssumeRole from the account A role's ARN
explanation: For cross-account access to a resource with a resource-based policy, the resource owner must allow the external principal in the bucket policy and the principal's own account must also allow the action in an identity-based policy. Buckets do not have trust policies; trust policies belong to roles. SCPs only restrict principals in their own organization and never grant access, and S3 buckets are not shared through AWS RAM.

question: An application on Amazon EC2 writes items to an Amazon DynamoDB table. The developers currently keep an IAM user's access key and secret access key in a configuration file on the instance. Which change is MOST secure?
options: Create an IAM role with the required DynamoDB permissions and attach it to the instance through an instance profile.
Move the access keys from the configuration file into the instance user data and rotate them every 90 days with a scheduled script.
Create a separate IAM user for each instance with only DynamoDB write permissions and bake that user's access keys into the AMI.
Store the access keys in an S3 bucket encrypted with SSE-S3 and have the instance download them at startup through a gateway endpoint.
explanation: An instance profile delivers temporary, automatically rotated role credentials to the instance through the metadata service, so no long-term keys are stored anywhere. User data, AMIs, and S3 downloads all still rely on long-term access keys that can leak and must be rotated manually.

question: A developer has permission to call ec2:RunInstances and can launch instances successfully. When the developer tries to launch an instance with an IAM instance profile attached, the request fails with an authorization error. What permission must be added to the developer's policy?
options: iam:PassRole for the role that is contained in the instance profile
sts:AssumeRole for the role that is contained in the instance profile
iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole for the Amazon EC2 service
iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy for the role that is contained in the instance profile
explanation: To give a role to an AWS service, such as attaching it to an EC2 instance, the caller needs iam:PassRole on that role, which prevents users from handing services more privileges than they have themselves. sts:AssumeRole would let the developer use the role directly, which is not what the launch requires. Service-linked roles are unrelated to instance profiles, and changing the trust policy is neither needed nor safe.

question: An administrator notices a role named AWSServiceRoleForElasticLoadBalancing in an account and wants to reduce its permissions to follow the principle of least privilege. What should a solutions architect advise?
options: Detach the AWS managed policy from the role and attach a customer managed policy that grants only the Elastic Load Balancing actions the account uses.
Attach a permissions boundary to the role that allows only the Elastic Load Balancing actions in use, so its effective permissions become the intersection.
It is a service-linked role: its permissions are defined by the service and cannot be edited, and it can be deleted only after the service stops using it.
Attach an SCP to the account that denies the unneeded Elastic Load Balancing actions, because SCPs restrict every role in a member account.
explanation: Service-linked roles are created and owned by an AWS service, include exactly the permissions the service needs, and their permissions and trust policies cannot be modified by the account owner. You cannot swap their policies or add boundaries to them. SCPs do not affect service-linked roles, so they cannot be used to restrict them either.

question: A solutions architect is reviewing how different workloads authenticate to AWS. In which scenarios should an IAM role with temporary credentials be used instead of an IAM user with long-term access keys? (Select THREE.)
options: Employees who sign in through the corporate SAML identity provider to use the AWS Management Console
A legacy third-party tool that supports only a static access key ID and secret access key
An AWS Lambda function that writes items to an Amazon DynamoDB table
An on-premises script that runs where no form of temporary credential retrieval is possible
Engineers from a partner's AWS account who need temporary access to troubleshoot resources
A break-glass identity that must work even when the corporate identity provider is unavailable
explanation: AWS services such as Lambda, cross-account partners, and federated workforce users should all obtain temporary credentials by assuming roles. A tool that only accepts static keys, an emergency break-glass identity that cannot depend on the IdP, and a script that truly cannot retrieve temporary credentials are the narrow cases where an IAM user may still be justified, ideally with tight permissions, MFA where possible, and key rotation.

question: A company grants a third-party monitoring SaaS provider access to its AWS account through a cross-account IAM role. The security team is concerned that another customer of the provider could trick the provider into using this role on that customer's behalf. Which solution addresses this confused deputy risk?
options: Create an IAM user for the provider instead of a role and require MFA on every API call, so only the provider's own staff can use the credentials.
Add an aws:SourceIp condition with the provider's published IP ranges to the role's trust policy so that only the provider's platform can assume it.
Share the role with the provider's AWS account through AWS RAM instead of using a trust policy, so only that specific account can use it.
Require a unique external ID in the role's trust policy with the sts:ExternalId condition, and have the provider supply it when assuming the role.
explanation: An external ID that is unique to each customer ensures the provider assumes the role only when acting for this customer, which mitigates the confused deputy problem. An IAM user with long-term keys is less secure and does not address the issue. The provider's IP addresses are shared by all its customers, so a source IP condition does not distinguish them, and IAM roles cannot be shared through AWS RAM.

question: Developers sign in to a central identity account with IAM users. They need to switch to an Admin role in a separate production account when performing releases. Which configuration enables this?
options: Create IAM users with matching names in the production account and enable password synchronization so the developers sign in once for both accounts.
Trust the identity account in the production role's trust policy, and grant the developers iam:PassRole on the role's ARN in the identity account.
Trust the identity account in the production role's trust policy, and grant the developers sts:AssumeRole on that role from the identity account.
Attach the production Admin role's permissions policy directly to the developers' IAM group in the identity account so they inherit the same access.
explanation: Cross-account role switching requires both sides: the role's trust policy must trust the source account (or specific principals), and the source principals need permission to call sts:AssumeRole on that role. IAM has no password synchronization between accounts. iam:PassRole is for handing a role to a service, and permissions policies in one account cannot grant access to resources in another account by themselves.

question: A security team wants to reduce the permissions of dozens of IAM roles by removing access to services and actions that the roles have not used in the last 90 days. Which approach meets this requirement with the LEAST effort?
options: Use AWS Trusted Advisor security checks to find over-permissive roles and have it automatically remove the unused permissions from every role.
Use IAM last accessed information and IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings to identify unused services and actions, then tighten the policies.
Enable CloudTrail Insights on the account so that it detects permissions unused for 90 days and removes them from the affected roles.
Download the IAM credential report, which shows the services and actions each role has used and when each one was last used.
explanation: IAM last accessed information shows when services and many actions were last used, and Access Analyzer unused access findings highlight unused roles, keys, and permissions, which makes right-sizing policies straightforward. Trusted Advisor does not edit policies, and CloudTrail Insights detects unusual API activity rather than unused permissions. The credential report lists IAM users and their credentials, not role permission usage.

question: A company has more than 50 project teams that share one AWS account. Engineers must be able to start and stop only the EC2 instances that belong to their own project, and new projects are added every month. The company wants to avoid writing a new policy for each project. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create an IAM group for each project with a policy that lists the ARNs of that project's instances, and add each engineer to their own project's group.
Place each project's instances in a separate VPC and use security group rules that allow only that project's engineers to manage them.
Create an AWS Resource Groups group for each project and grant engineers iam:PassRole for their project's group to scope instance actions.
Tag principals and instances with a project tag and use a policy condition that requires aws:ResourceTag/project to match aws:PrincipalTag/project.
explanation: Attribute-based access control compares tags on the principal with tags on the resource, so one policy works for every current and future project. Per-project groups with instance ARNs require constant policy updates. Security groups control network traffic, not EC2 API calls, and Resource Groups combined with iam:PassRole do not restrict instance actions.

question: A company has 30 sandbox accounts and 12 production accounts in AWS Organizations. Sandbox accounts need one set of restrictions and production accounts need a different set. The company wants to manage as few policy attachments as possible, including for accounts added later. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Place the accounts in separate sandbox and production OUs and attach the appropriate SCPs to each OU.
Attach the appropriate SCPs directly to each of the 42 member accounts and to new accounts as they are created.
Create IAM groups named sandbox and production in the management account and attach the policies to them.
Tag each account as sandbox or production and attach the SCPs to the tag keys in the organization.
explanation: Organizational units group accounts so that a policy attached to an OU is inherited by every account in it, including accounts moved in later. Attaching SCPs to every account multiplies the work. IAM groups in the management account do not apply to other accounts, and SCPs are attached to the root, OUs, or accounts, not to tags.

question: A company must ensure that Amazon S3 buckets in all of its member accounts can never be accessed by principals outside its organization, even if a developer writes a bucket policy that grants access to an external account. The control must be centrally enforced. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies all S3 actions unless aws:PrincipalOrgID matches the organization ID, so principals outside the organization are blocked from every bucket.
Deploy an AWS Config organization rule to every account that detects bucket policies granting external access and notifies the security team through Amazon SNS.
Attach a resource control policy (RCP) to the organization root that denies S3 access when aws:PrincipalOrgID does not match the organization ID, exempting required AWS service principals.
Enable IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust and configure it to automatically delete any bucket policy statement that grants access to an external account.
explanation: RCPs set the maximum permissions on resources in member accounts regardless of who calls them, so they can block external principals even when a bucket policy allows them. SCPs restrict only principals inside the organization's accounts and have no effect on external callers. A Config rule only detects and notifies, and Access Analyzer reports external access findings but does not delete policies.

question: A security team is designing its service control policy (SCP) strategy for AWS Organizations. Which statements about SCPs are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: SCPs affect all IAM users and roles in member accounts, including each member account's root user.
An allow in an account's IAM policy can override a deny in an SCP attached to the account's OU.
SCPs restrict the permissions of service-linked roles in member accounts.
SCPs restrict users and roles in the management account of the organization.
SCPs never grant permissions; identities still need IAM policies that allow the actions.
explanation: SCPs only define the maximum available permissions, so IAM policies must still grant access, and they apply to every principal in member accounts, including the root user. SCPs do not affect service-linked roles or principals in the management account, which is one reason to keep workloads out of the management account. An explicit deny from an SCP cannot be overridden by any IAM allow.

question: A company federates all workforce access to its AWS accounts through IAM Identity Center with an external identity provider. Leadership is concerned that an outage of the identity provider would lock administrators out of AWS during an incident. Which approach provides resilient emergency access while following security best practices?
options: Share the management account's root user credentials with all administrators so they can sign in if the identity provider fails.
Configure IAM Identity Center to bypass the external identity provider automatically whenever the provider is unreachable.
Create a small number of break-glass IAM users with strong passwords and hardware MFA, store the credentials securely, and alert on every use.
Remove the MFA requirement from all administrator permission sets so that administrators can sign in faster through the identity provider during incidents.
explanation: A tightly controlled set of break-glass IAM users with MFA does not depend on the external IdP, and monitoring their use keeps them auditable. Sharing root credentials widely is a serious security risk. Identity Center has no automatic bypass of its configured identity source, and removing MFA weakens security without addressing an IdP outage.

question: A company must ensure that every account in its Production OU backs up resources tagged backup=daily every day, keeps the backups for 35 days, and copies them to a second Region. Account administrators must not be able to opt out, and the setup must apply automatically to new production accounts. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Attach an SCP to the Production OU that requires every account to create daily EBS and RDS snapshots with 35-day retention and a cross-Region copy.
Create a backup vault with a 35-day retention Vault Lock in the management account and share it with the Production OU accounts through AWS RAM.
Ask each account owner to create an AWS Backup plan with a daily rule and a cross-Region copy, and verify compliance monthly by using AWS Cost Explorer.
Attach an AWS Organizations backup policy to the Production OU that defines an AWS Backup plan with a daily rule, 35-day retention, and a cross-Region copy action.
explanation: Backup policies in AWS Organizations centrally define AWS Backup plans, including schedules, retention, and cross-Region copies, and apply them to every account in the target OU, including new ones. SCPs can only allow or deny actions and cannot create backups. Sharing a vault does not schedule backups, and relying on account owners with a cost tool for verification is manual and unreliable.

question: A company has 12 AWS accounts that are each billed separately. The company plans to create an organization in AWS Organizations and enable consolidated billing. Which benefits will consolidated billing provide? (Select TWO.)
options: Member accounts can no longer view their own costs in Cost Explorer, which reduces the risk of billing data exposure across teams.
Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts purchased in one account can apply to eligible usage in other accounts.
Data transfer between accounts in the organization becomes free of charge, because all of the accounts share one payer account.
Usage across all accounts is combined to qualify for volume pricing tiers, such as tiered Amazon S3 storage pricing.
SCPs are created automatically to stop resources in any member account that exceeds its share of the consolidated bill.
explanation: Consolidated billing gives one bill for all accounts, aggregates usage for volume discounts, and shares Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts across accounts by default. Data transfer is still charged normally between accounts. Member accounts can still see their own costs, and Organizations does not create cost-based SCPs automatically.

question: A company is setting up IAM Identity Center so that employees can access several AWS accounts. What does a permission set represent in IAM Identity Center?
options: A service control policy that Identity Center attaches to the OUs containing the assigned accounts to define what users can do there
An IAM group that Identity Center creates in the management account, adding assigned users so they inherit its policies in every account
A SAML assertion attribute that maps each workforce user to a matching IAM user that Identity Center provisions in each assigned account
A collection of policies that Identity Center provisions as an IAM role in each account where the permission set is assigned
explanation: A permission set is a template of AWS managed, customer managed, or inline policies (and optionally a permissions boundary); when it is assigned to an account, Identity Center creates a corresponding IAM role there that users assume through single sign-on. It is not an SCP, an IAM group, or a mapping to IAM users, since Identity Center users never need IAM users in the member accounts.

question: A company uses Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) on premises. Employees must access the AWS Management Console of a single AWS account with their corporate credentials, and the company does not want to create IAM users. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create IAM users whose names match the Active Directory user names and synchronize their passwords from AD FS with a scheduled script so employees reuse corporate credentials.
Configure AD FS as a SAML 2.0 identity provider in IAM and create IAM roles that trust it, so users receive role credentials through AssumeRoleWithSAML.
Create an IAM OIDC identity provider for AD FS and attach a permissions policy directly to the identity provider so federated users receive those permissions at sign-in.
Use Amazon Cognito user pools federated with AD FS to replicate the Active Directory users into IAM users in the account, which then sign in to the console.
explanation: SAML 2.0 federation lets AD FS authenticate users and pass a SAML assertion to AWS, which maps users to IAM roles through AssumeRoleWithSAML and signs them in to the console with temporary credentials. Synchronizing IAM users creates the long-term identities the company wants to avoid. Permissions cannot be attached to an identity provider; federated users always receive permissions by assuming a role, and Cognito user pools do not create IAM users.

question: A payment application on Amazon EC2 sends its logs to a CloudWatch Logs log group. The operations team must be notified by email when the text PaymentFailed appears more than 10 times within 5 minutes. Which combination of steps meets this requirement? (Select TWO.)
options: Create a subscription filter that sends all log events to Amazon S3 and query them with Amazon Athena every 5 minutes.
Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for the log group and alarm on the number of events recorded.
Create a metric filter on the log group that matches PaymentFailed and publishes a custom metric.
Increase the log group's retention period so that CloudWatch counts PaymentFailed messages automatically.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the custom metric with a threshold of 10 over a 5-minute period that notifies an SNS topic.
explanation: A metric filter turns matching log events into a CloudWatch metric, and an alarm on that metric with an SNS action sends the email when the threshold is crossed. CloudTrail records API calls, not application log contents. Scheduled Athena queries add latency and operational overhead, and retention settings only control how long logs are kept.

question: A company stores application logs in CloudWatch Logs log groups that use the default retention setting. Engineers need the logs for only 30 days for troubleshooting, but compliance requires keeping an archive for 1 year at the lowest possible cost. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Keep the default retention, which never expires log events, and run a yearly script that deletes log streams older than 1 year from each log group.
Set log group retention to 30 days and deliver the logs to Amazon S3 with a lifecycle rule that moves them to an archive class and expires them after 1 year.
Set the retention period of every log group to 1 year and keep all logs in CloudWatch Logs so engineers and auditors query the same data in one place.
Send the application logs to AWS CloudTrail and use the CloudTrail event history, which has no storage charge, as the 1-year compliance archive.
explanation: Short CloudWatch Logs retention keeps CloudWatch Logs storage costs low, and archiving to S3 with a lifecycle rule to a low-cost archive class meets the 1-year requirement cheaply. By default log groups never expire, so costs grow indefinitely and manual deletion adds overhead. Keeping a full year in CloudWatch Logs costs more than S3 archive storage, and CloudTrail does not store application logs.

question: During an incident, engineers need to interactively search and aggregate application logs across several CloudWatch Logs log groups, for example to find the 10 slowest requests in the last hour. They want results in seconds without moving the data elsewhere. Which feature should they use?
options: An export of the logs to Amazon S3 followed by loading them into Amazon Redshift
Metric filters for every log field displayed on a CloudWatch dashboard
CloudTrail Lake queries run against the application log groups
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries run against the log groups
explanation: CloudWatch Logs Insights provides a purpose-built query language to filter, parse, and aggregate log data across log groups in place. Exporting to S3 and loading Redshift is slow for interactive troubleshooting. Metric filters need to be defined in advance and cannot answer ad hoc questions, and CloudTrail Lake stores CloudTrail and other activity events, not CloudWatch application log groups.

question: A security team must receive application logs from CloudWatch Logs in 50 workload accounts in near real time and store them in a central logging account for analysis. The solution must scale without per-account custom code. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Run a daily CreateExportTask job in each account that exports the log groups to an S3 bucket in the logging account, using a bucket policy for cross-account writes.
Enable CloudWatch cross-account observability with the logging account as the monitoring account so that log data is copied into storage there.
Create subscription filters that send the log events to a cross-account CloudWatch Logs destination backed by Amazon Data Firehose in the logging account.
Configure an organization trail in AWS CloudTrail with CloudWatch Logs delivery so the application log groups are forwarded to the logging account.
explanation: Subscription filters stream log events in near real time, and a cross-account destination backed by Firehose can deliver them to S3 or another analytics store in the logging account. Export tasks are batch jobs that do not meet the near-real-time requirement. Cross-account observability lets a monitoring account view source account data but does not copy it into central storage, and CloudTrail delivers API activity, not application logs.

question: An auditor needs to know which IAM principal terminated an Amazon EC2 instance 3 days ago. The account has never had a CloudTrail trail configured. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Search the CloudTrail Event history, which retains the last 90 days of management events by default.
Accept that the information is unavailable because CloudTrail records nothing until a trail is created.
Review the VPC Flow Logs for the subnet to find the TerminateInstances API call.
Review the instance's StatusCheckFailed metric in CloudWatch to identify who stopped it.
explanation: CloudTrail is enabled by default for every account, and Event history provides 90 days of management events such as TerminateInstances with the calling identity. A trail is needed only for longer retention, data events, or delivery to S3 and CloudWatch Logs. Flow Logs capture network traffic metadata, not API calls, and CloudWatch metrics do not record who made a change.

question: A company must record every GetObject and PutObject call made against an S3 bucket that holds sensitive customer documents, including which principal made each call. The company already has a CloudTrail trail that logs management events. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Keep the existing configuration, because management events already include S3 object-level calls.
Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket so that each object version records who accessed it.
Configure the trail to log S3 data events for the bucket.
Enable CloudTrail Insights events on the existing trail.
explanation: Object-level operations such as GetObject and PutObject are data events, which are not logged by default and must be enabled on a trail (they incur additional charges). Management events cover control-plane operations such as CreateBucket or PutBucketPolicy. Versioning keeps object versions but does not log reads, and Insights detects unusual API activity rather than recording each object access.

question: A company with 80 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations must log API activity from all Regions in every account, including accounts created in the future, to a central S3 bucket. Administrators of member accounts must not be able to stop or modify this logging. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create a multi-Region organization trail from the management account or a delegated administrator account that delivers to an S3 bucket in a log archive account.
Deploy a multi-Region trail to each account with CloudFormation StackSets and grant account administrators permission to manage their own trail.
Rely on CloudTrail Event history in each account, which covers every Region, and export it to the central bucket with a monthly script.
Create a single-Region trail in the management account that delivers to the central bucket and logs activity for the management account only.
explanation: An organization trail automatically applies to all current and future member accounts, and member accounts can see it but cannot modify or delete it; a multi-Region trail captures every Region, and a separate log archive account protects the logs. Per-account trails managed by account admins can be stopped. Event history keeps only 90 days of management events, and a single-account, single-Region trail misses most activity.

question: Auditors require proof that CloudTrail log files delivered to Amazon S3 have not been modified or deleted after delivery. Which feature should the company enable?
options: Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS) for the CloudTrail log files, with a key policy that restricts decryption
CloudTrail log file integrity validation, then validate the logs by using the generated digest files
CloudTrail Insights events on the trail to detect tampering with the delivered log files in the bucket
S3 server access logging on the log bucket, which records the requests that modify or delete CloudTrail log files
explanation: Log file integrity validation creates hourly digest files that contain SHA-256 hashes of the delivered log files and are signed by CloudTrail, so any modification or deletion can be detected. KMS encryption protects confidentiality but does not prove integrity. Insights detects unusual API call rates, and server access logs record requests to the bucket without proving that files are unchanged.

question: A company centralizes CloudTrail logs from all accounts in an S3 bucket in a log archive account. The security team wants the logs to be confidential, tamper-evident, and protected from deletion for 7 years, even by administrators. Which actions should a solutions architect take? (Select THREE.)
options: Encrypt the log files with SSE-KMS by using a customer managed key with a restrictive key policy.
Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the log bucket with a 7-year retention period.
Change the trail to a single-Region trail to reduce the number of log files.
Store the logs in each workload account so that local administrators can manage retention.
Enable log file integrity validation on the trail.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the log bucket.
explanation: Integrity validation makes tampering detectable, SSE-KMS with a restricted customer managed key limits who can decrypt the logs, and Object Lock in compliance mode prevents anyone, including the root user, from deleting or overwriting objects during retention. Transfer Acceleration only speeds up transfers. Keeping logs in workload accounts gives local admins control over them, and a single-Region trail loses visibility into other Regions.

question: A central IT team wants developers to self-provision approved Amazon EMR clusters and Amazon RDS databases that already meet company standards. Developers must not receive broad IAM permissions to create these resources directly. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Publish the configurations as AWS Service Catalog products in a portfolio, grant developers access to it, and add a launch constraint with an IAM role that can create the resources.
Store approved CloudFormation templates in an S3 bucket and grant developers AdministratorAccess so they can deploy those templates with AWS CloudFormation.
Create the EMR clusters and RDS databases centrally in a shared services account and share them with the developers' accounts through AWS RAM resource shares.
Use AWS Control Tower Account Factory to provision a new account that already contains the approved EMR cluster and RDS database for each developer request.
explanation: Service Catalog lets administrators publish approved products, and a launch constraint makes Service Catalog use a specified role to provision them, so end users need only Service Catalog permissions. Granting AdministratorAccess violates least privilege. AWS RAM shares specific resource types such as subnets, not EMR clusters or RDS instances, and Account Factory vends accounts rather than individual resources.

question: A company gives each development team a sandbox account. When a sandbox account's forecasted monthly spend exceeds USD 1,000, the company wants to automatically prevent the team from launching new Amazon EC2 instances while leaving existing workloads running. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create a budget in AWS Budgets with a forecasted-cost threshold and a budget action that applies an SCP denying ec2:RunInstances to the account.
Configure AWS Cost Explorer forecasting for the account so that it blocks new EC2 launches once forecasted spend exceeds USD 1,000.
Create a CloudWatch billing alarm on EstimatedCharges that invokes a Lambda function to terminate every EC2 instance in the account at the threshold.
Use AWS Cost Anomaly Detection with a monitor for the account to automatically delete newly launched instances that cause unusual spending.
explanation: Budget actions can run automatically when an actual or forecasted threshold is crossed and can apply an IAM policy or SCP, or stop specific EC2 or RDS instances. Cost Explorer is for analysis and cannot enforce controls. Terminating every instance would disrupt existing workloads, and Cost Anomaly Detection only sends alerts.

question: A finance team wants to visualize the company's AWS costs for the last 12 months grouped by service and linked account, and to see a forecast for the next 3 months. The team does not want to build any data pipelines. Which AWS tool should the team use?
options: AWS Budgets
AWS Data Exports with Amazon Athena
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Cost Explorer
explanation: Cost Explorer provides ready-made graphs of historical costs that can be grouped and filtered by service, account, tags, and more, and includes cost forecasts. Budgets tracks spending against thresholds rather than providing historical analysis. Data Exports with Athena requires setting up exports and queries, and Trusted Advisor gives best-practice recommendations rather than cost reports.

question: A company needs the most detailed AWS billing data available, including hourly line items with resource IDs, to build a custom chargeback model that analysts will query with SQL. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Download the monthly invoice PDF from the Billing and Cost Management console and load its line items into Amazon Redshift.
Create a standard export in AWS Data Exports (CUR 2.0) that delivers to Amazon S3 and query it with Amazon Athena.
Export the 12-month cost graph from AWS Cost Explorer to a CSV file each month and load it into an Amazon RDS database for SQL.
Schedule an AWS Budgets report that emails daily spending per service to the analysts, who import it into a SQL database.
explanation: Data Exports delivers the Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0) with line-item detail, hourly granularity, and resource IDs to S3, where Athena can query it with SQL. Invoices and Budgets reports are summaries. Cost Explorer CSV exports are aggregated and do not provide the full line-item detail needed for chargeback.

question: A company tags all of its resources with a CostCenter tag. In AWS Cost Explorer, the finance team cannot filter or group costs by CostCenter. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Enable AWS Config in every account so that resource tag values are recorded and passed to Cost Explorer as billing dimensions.
Apply the CostCenter tag to the IAM users and roles that created the resources so that their costs roll up under that tag.
Activate CostCenter as a user-defined cost allocation tag in the Billing and Cost Management console of the management account.
Wait for the next billing cycle, because new tags appear in Cost Explorer only after a full month of tagged usage has been billed.
explanation: User-defined tags must be activated as cost allocation tags, in the management (payer) account for an organization, before they appear in Cost Explorer and cost reports; after activation it can take up to 24 hours, and activation applies only going forward unless the management account requests a backfill of up to 12 months. AWS Config records resource configurations, not billing dimensions. Tagging the creator does not tag the resources' costs, and no full-month wait is required.

question: A company with 40 accounts in AWS Organizations allocates costs by a Project tag, but teams use inconsistent values such as proj-a, ProjectA, and project_a, and some EC2 instances are launched with no Project tag at all. Which combination of actions will enforce consistent cost allocation tagging? (Select TWO.)
options: Create a tag policy in AWS Organizations that defines the allowed key capitalization and values for the Project tag and enforces them for selected resource types.
Share the Project tag key and its allowed values with all member accounts by using an AWS RAM resource share from the management account.
Use AWS Cost Explorer to merge and rename the inconsistent Project tag values on resources across all accounts in the organization.
Attach an SCP that denies ec2:RunInstances when the aws:RequestTag/Project condition key is missing from the request.
Create an AWS Budgets budget with a budget action that automatically adds the missing Project tag to untagged EC2 instances.
explanation: Tag policies standardize tag keys and allowed values and can prevent noncompliant tag operations on supported resource types, while an SCP with a Null or missing aws:RequestTag condition blocks launches without the tag. Budgets cannot modify tags. Cost Explorer reports on tags but does not rename them on resources, and tag keys are not resources that can be shared through AWS RAM.

question: A company has 60 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations, and its workforce identities are managed in Microsoft Entra ID. Employees need single sign-on to the accounts with different permission levels per account, and users must be provisioned and deprovisioned automatically when they join or leave. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an IAM SAML identity provider and federated roles in each of the 60 accounts, trusting Entra ID, and update every account whenever new roles are needed.
Enable IAM Identity Center, connect Entra ID as an external identity provider with SAML 2.0 and SCIM provisioning, and assign permission sets to groups per account.
Create IAM users for all employees in the management account and let them switch into permission-specific roles in each member account.
Deploy Simple AD in every account, synchronize the employees from Entra ID into each directory, and use it for console sign-in per account.
explanation: IAM Identity Center provides central single sign-on across all accounts in the organization, SCIM keeps users and groups synchronized from Entra ID automatically, and permission sets define access per account. Per-account SAML providers and roles work but multiply the administration across 60 accounts. IAM users require manual lifecycle management, and Simple AD does not synchronize from Entra ID or provide multi-account access.

question: A company is starting its multi-account journey. It wants a well-architected landing zone with a centralized log archive account and an audit account, preconfigured governance controls, and a self-service way to create new accounts that comply with company standards, with the LEAST effort. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create the organization, OUs, trails, and AWS Config rules manually with scripts in every new account.
Use AWS Service Catalog on its own to create new AWS accounts from a portfolio of templates.
Share a landing zone from the management account with new accounts by using AWS RAM.
Set up AWS Control Tower and use Account Factory to provision new accounts.
explanation: AWS Control Tower automates a landing zone on top of AWS Organizations, including log archive and audit accounts, enables governance controls, and provides Account Factory for standardized account vending. Scripting everything manually adds significant effort and drift risk. Account Factory itself is built on Service Catalog, but Service Catalog alone does not set up a governed landing zone, and AWS RAM cannot share a landing zone.

question: A security team uses AWS Control Tower to govern its organization. Which statements correctly describe how Control Tower controls are implemented? (Select TWO.)
options: Detective controls are implemented as AWS Config rules that flag noncompliant resources.
Proactive controls are enforced by Amazon GuardDuty findings after resources are created.
Detective controls block noncompliant API calls before the calls are allowed to run.
Controls can be applied only to the management account, not to OUs or member accounts.
Preventive controls are enforced through organization policies such as service control policies.
explanation: Control Tower preventive controls use organization policies such as SCPs to stop disallowed actions, and detective controls use AWS Config rules to detect noncompliance after the fact. Proactive controls use CloudFormation hooks to check resources before they are provisioned, not GuardDuty. Detective controls do not block calls, and controls are enabled on OUs so they apply to the accounts within them.

question: A networking account in an organization owns a VPC with shared subnets and a transit gateway. Application accounts must launch EC2 instances directly into the central subnets, and other accounts must attach their own VPCs to the transit gateway, so the company can avoid duplicate NAT gateways and a VPC peering mesh. Which resources should the networking account share by using AWS RAM? (Select TWO.)
options: The VPC's internet gateway
The transit gateway
The NAT gateways' Elastic IP addresses
The VPC subnets
IAM roles for each application team
explanation: AWS RAM supports sharing VPC subnets, which lets participant accounts launch resources into centrally managed subnets that use shared NAT gateways, and sharing transit gateways so other accounts can create attachments. Internet gateways, Elastic IP addresses, and IAM roles are not shared through AWS RAM; access to roles is granted through trust policies instead.

question: A compliance officer must give external auditors copies of AWS's SOC 2 report and PCI DSS attestation of compliance, and must review and accept a Business Associate Addendum (BAA) for the company's account. Which AWS service provides this?
options: AWS Audit Manager
AWS Artifact
AWS Config
AWS Security Hub
explanation: AWS Artifact is the self-service portal for downloading AWS compliance reports such as SOC and PCI attestations and for accepting agreements such as the BAA. Audit Manager collects evidence about the customer's own use of AWS for audits. Config records resource configuration compliance, and Security Hub aggregates security findings.

question: A company brings its own Microsoft SQL Server licenses, which are licensed per vCPU, to Amazon EC2 across several accounts in its organization. Licensed usage must never exceed 200 vCPUs, and launches that would exceed the limit must be blocked. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create an AWS License Manager license configuration with a 200-vCPU hard limit, associate it with the SQL Server AMIs, and share it across the accounts.
Use Service Quotas to lower each account's Running On-Demand Standard instances vCPU quota so the organization-wide total stays under 200 vCPUs.
Create an AWS Budgets budget filtered to SQL Server usage that sends an alert when spending exceeds the cost of 200 vCPUs.
Tag SQL Server instances with their vCPU count, aggregate the tags in AWS Cost Explorer, and review the organization-wide total each week.
explanation: License Manager tracks license usage against rules such as vCPU counts, and a hard limit blocks launches of associated AMIs that would exceed the license count; the configuration can be shared across accounts in the organization. Service Quotas limits all instance usage, not SQL Server licenses specifically. Budgets and Cost Explorer only report on spending after the fact and cannot block launches.

question: A central operations team in a monitoring account must view metrics, logs, and traces from 30 workload accounts in the same organization from one place, without switching roles into each account. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Write an AWS Lambda function in each workload account that copies metrics, logs, and traces to the monitoring account every minute.
Create an organization trail with CloudWatch Logs delivery so that metrics, logs, and traces from every account appear in the monitoring account.
Assign the team an IAM Identity Center permission set in every account and open each account's dashboards separately.
Configure CloudWatch cross-account observability with the monitoring account as the sink and link the workload accounts as source accounts.
explanation: CloudWatch cross-account observability lets a monitoring account search and visualize metrics, logs, and traces from linked source accounts, and accounts can be linked through AWS Organizations. Custom copy functions add code and cost. An organization trail centralizes API activity, not metrics and traces, and signing in to each account separately is what the team wants to avoid.

question: A company has 75 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations. The security team must continuously identify S3 buckets, KMS keys, IAM roles, and SQS queues whose resource-based policies grant access to principals outside the organization, and must review each case as a finding. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Enable Amazon Macie in every account and review its findings for buckets that contain sensitive data.
Enable Amazon GuardDuty with an organization administrator and review findings about unusual API calls.
Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust in each Region that has resources.
Run a weekly AWS Lambda function that downloads every resource policy and searches it for account IDs that are not in the organization.
explanation: An IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer uses logic-based reasoning on resource-based policies and generates a finding for each supported resource shared outside the zone of trust; with the organization as the zone of trust, only access from outside the organization is reported. External access analysis is Regional, so an analyzer is needed in each Region with resources. Macie discovers sensitive data in S3, GuardDuty detects threats from activity, and a custom Lambda scanner adds code to maintain and misses the reasoning that Access Analyzer performs.

question: A platform team stores IAM policies in a Git repository and deploys them through a CI/CD pipeline. The pipeline must fail automatically if a changed policy grants any access that the currently deployed version does not grant, or if any policy allows the iam:CreateUser or kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion actions. Which IAM Access Analyzer checks should the pipeline run? (Select TWO.)
options: CheckNoNewAccess, comparing each updated policy with the currently deployed version
StartPolicyGeneration, generating a policy from the last 90 days of CloudTrail activity
GenerateCredentialReport, listing the credential status of every IAM user
CheckAccessNotGranted, verifying that the policy does not allow the listed critical actions
StartResourceScan, rescanning resources that are reported in existing external access findings
explanation: IAM Access Analyzer custom policy checks validate policies against your own security standards: CheckNoNewAccess reports whether an updated policy grants new access compared to the existing version, and CheckAccessNotGranted reports whether specified critical actions are allowed. Both can be called from the CLI or API, which makes them suitable as pipeline gates. Policy generation builds a policy from CloudTrail activity, the credential report lists IAM user credentials, and a resource rescan only refreshes external access findings for deployed resources.

question: An IAM role used by a batch application was created two years ago with several broad AWS managed policies. The account has a CloudTrail trail that has logged management events for the entire period. The security team wants to replace the broad policies with a least-privilege policy based on the actions the role actually used, with the LEAST effort. What should the team do?
options: Download the IAM credential report and copy the services listed for the role into a new customer managed policy.
Enable AWS Trusted Advisor security checks for the account and apply the least-privilege policy that Trusted Advisor recommends for the role.
Write CloudTrail Lake queries for every API call made by the role and hand-build a policy from the query results.
Use IAM Access Analyzer policy generation to build a policy template from the role's CloudTrail activity, then review and attach it.
explanation: IAM Access Analyzer policy generation analyzes CloudTrail events for a user or role over a period of up to 90 days and produces a policy template with the services and actions used, which you can refine and attach as a managed policy. The credential report covers IAM users' credentials, not role activity. Trusted Advisor does not generate IAM policies, and hand-building a policy from CloudTrail queries is the same analysis with far more manual effort.

question: A multi-tenant SaaS application assumes a single IAM role that can read every tenant's prefix in a shared S3 bucket. For each request, the application must receive credentials that can read only the current tenant's prefix, without creating a role per tenant. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Pass an inline session policy that allows only the tenant's prefix when calling AssumeRole, so the session gets the intersection of the role policy and the session policy.
Attach a permissions boundary to the role that allows only one tenant prefix, and update the boundary with the current tenant's prefix before each AssumeRole call.
Create an IAM user for each tenant with a policy scoped to its prefix, and store each user's access keys in the application configuration file.
Add a deny statement for all other tenants' prefixes to the bucket policy, rewriting the bucket policy with the current tenant before each request.
explanation: Session policies are passed when a role session is created, and the session's permissions are the intersection of the role's identity-based policies and the session policy, so each session can be scoped down to one tenant without new roles. Session policies cannot add permissions. Updating a boundary or bucket policy per request is not safe for concurrent tenants and would affect every session at once, and per-tenant IAM users rely on long-term access keys.

question: In a single AWS account, an IAM user has no identity-based policies. An Amazon SQS queue in the same account has a queue policy that allows sqs:SendMessage for that IAM user's ARN. No SCPs, permissions boundaries, or deny statements apply. What happens when the user calls SendMessage on the queue?
options: The request is denied, because an identity-based policy and a resource-based policy must both allow the request before IAM authorizes it.
The request is denied, because resource-based policies such as queue policies grant access only to principals from other AWS accounts.
The request is allowed, because within the same account an allow in either the identity-based policy or the resource-based policy is sufficient.
The request is allowed only after the user calls sts:AssumeRole on a role named in the queue policy and sends the message with that role session.
explanation: For requests within a single account, AWS allows the request if either the identity-based policy or the resource-based policy allows it and no explicit deny applies. Requiring both allows is the rule for cross-account access, where the principal's account must also grant the permission. Resource-based policies can name principals in the same account, and no role assumption is needed when the queue policy names the user directly.

question: A company keeps shared reference data in an S3 bucket. Principals in every account of the company's organization, including accounts that will be created later, must be able to read the objects. No one outside the organization may read them. Which bucket policy approach meets these requirements with the LEAST maintenance?
options: List every member account ID as a principal in the bucket policy and add new account IDs whenever an account is created.
Allow s3:GetObject for Principal "*" with a condition that aws:PrincipalOrgID equals the organization ID.
Allow s3:GetObject only when aws:SourceIp matches the CIDR ranges of every VPC in the organization.
Allow s3:GetObject for Principal "*" and enable S3 Block Public Access on the bucket to block outsiders.
explanation: The aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key compares the requester's organization ID with the value in the policy, so a single statement covers all member accounts, and accounts added or removed later are handled automatically. Listing account IDs requires constant updates. Source IP conditions do not identify accounts, and requests through VPC endpoints do not carry public source IPs. A policy with Principal "*" and no restricting condition is public, which Block Public Access would reject rather than scope to the organization.

question: The cloud security team manages service control policies and tag policies for an organization by signing in to the management account every day. The company wants to follow AWS best practices by minimizing the use of the management account while letting the security team keep managing these policies. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Create IAM users with MFA for the security team in the management account and restrict their sign-in to business hours with an aws:CurrentTime condition.
Share the management account's administrator role with the security team's member account through AWS RAM so they no longer sign in there.
Move the security team's workloads into the management account so that the team works in only one account and policy changes stay central.
Create a resource-based delegation policy in AWS Organizations that delegates policy management to the security team's member account.
explanation: AWS Organizations lets the management account delegate policy management, which is otherwise available only to the management account, to specified member accounts through a resource-based delegation policy. AWS recommends using the management account only for tasks that require it, partly because SCPs do not restrict principals in the management account. IAM users in the management account still use it daily, IAM roles cannot be shared through AWS RAM, and running workloads in the management account goes against best practice.

question: A company must guarantee that no Amazon Machine Image (AMI) or Amazon EBS snapshot in any of its 300 accounts can be shared publicly. The baseline must apply to new accounts automatically, must keep working when EC2 introduces new API actions, and must also govern actions taken by service-linked roles. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Attach an EC2 declarative policy to the organization root that sets image block public access and snapshot block public access.
Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies ec2:ModifyImageAttribute and ec2:ModifySnapshotAttribute, the API actions that change sharing settings.
Deploy an AWS Config rule with automatic remediation that makes public AMIs and snapshots private after they are detected.
Create a tag policy that requires a Public=false tag on every AMI and EBS snapshot and enforces it for the ec2:image and ec2:snapshot resource types.
explanation: Declarative policies are enforced in the service control plane rather than by authorizing API calls, so the configuration persists when the service adds new features or APIs, applies to accounts that join later, and governs service-linked roles. EC2 declarative policies support image block public access and snapshot block public access. An SCP controls specific API actions and does not govern service-linked roles, a Config rule only remediates after the resource is already public, and a tag does not control sharing.

question: A company uses IAM Identity Center with its corporate directory as the identity source. Developers from 40 teams share one AWS account and need identical permissions, except that each developer may manage only the resources tagged with their own team's CostCenter value. Team membership changes often. Which solution requires the LEAST ongoing administration?
options: Create one permission set per team whose policy lists the ARNs of that team's resources, and reassign developers to a different permission set when they change teams.
Create an SCP for each team that denies access to resources tagged with other teams' CostCenter values, and attach all of the SCPs to the shared account.
Enable attributes for access control with the CostCenter user attribute and use one permission set whose policy matches aws:PrincipalTag/CostCenter to aws:ResourceTag/CostCenter.
Create an IAM user for each developer in the shared account, tag each user with their team's CostCenter value, and compare it with resource tags.
explanation: With ABAC in IAM Identity Center, user attributes from the identity source are passed into the AWS session as tags, so a single permission set can compare the principal's CostCenter tag with the resource's tag. When a developer changes teams, only the directory attribute changes. Per-team permission sets and SCPs multiply administration, and IAM users bypass the central identity source and require their own lifecycle management.

question: An administrator creates an IAM Identity Center permission set that references a customer managed policy named AppDeployPolicy. Assigning the permission set to a newly created member account fails, although the same assignment works in older accounts. What is the MOST likely cause, and how should it be fixed?
options: Customer managed policies can be referenced only from the management account, so the policy must be converted to an SCP attached to the new account.
The policy does not exist in the new account; create AppDeployPolicy with the same name and path in every account that receives the permission set.
Permission sets support only AWS managed policies, so the policy must be replaced with the closest AWS managed job function policy.
The new account has not accepted an AWS RAM invitation for the policy, so the invitation must be accepted in the new account.
explanation: When a permission set references a customer managed policy, IAM Identity Center attaches an existing IAM policy with the same name and path in each assigned account to the role it creates, so the policy must be created in every target account first, for example with CloudFormation StackSets. Inline and AWS managed policies do not need this step. Permission sets support customer managed policies, SCPs serve a different purpose, and IAM policies are not shared through AWS RAM.

question: A company wants employees to sign in to Amazon WorkSpaces and the AWS Management Console with their existing on-premises Active Directory credentials. User accounts and password policies must continue to be managed only on premises, no directory data may be synchronized to AWS, and sign-ins must use the company's existing RADIUS-based MFA. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Deploy AD Connector in a VPC that can reach the on-premises domain controllers and enable RADIUS MFA on the connector.
Deploy Simple AD in AWS, re-create the users in it, and enable RADIUS MFA on the Simple AD directory for WorkSpaces and console sign-in.
Deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD and replicate all users and passwords into it from the on-premises domain.
Create an Amazon Cognito user pool, import the users from Active Directory, and enable MFA in the user pool.
explanation: AD Connector is a proxy that forwards sign-in requests to the on-premises domain controllers, so users and policies stay on premises with no directory synchronization, and it can integrate with existing RADIUS-based MFA. Simple AD is a separate standalone directory and does not support MFA. Replicating users into a managed directory or a Cognito user pool contradicts the requirement to keep identity data only on premises.

question: A company is migrating .NET applications and Amazon RDS for SQL Server databases that use Windows authentication to AWS. It needs a real Microsoft Active Directory in AWS that survives the loss of an Availability Zone and that can trust the company's existing on-premises forest. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Deploy Simple AD across two subnets in different Availability Zones and create a two-way trust relationship with the on-premises forest.
Deploy AD Connector across two subnets in different Availability Zones and point the RDS for SQL Server instances at the connector for Windows authentication.
Install Active Directory Domain Services on a single large EC2 instance, enable EC2 automatic recovery, and create a forest trust from that domain.
Deploy AWS Managed Microsoft AD, which runs domain controllers in two Availability Zones, and create a trust with the on-premises forest.
explanation: AWS Managed Microsoft AD is an actual Windows Server Active Directory managed by AWS, deploys two domain controllers in different Availability Zones by default, supports trusts with existing domains, and works with RDS for SQL Server. Simple AD is Samba-based, does not support trusts, and is not compatible with RDS for SQL Server; AD Connector is also not compatible with RDS for SQL Server. A single self-managed domain controller is a single point of failure and adds patching and backup work.

question: A small company with 150 employees needs a directory in AWS for Amazon WorkSpaces and for LDAP authentication on a few Linux EC2 instances. It has no on-premises Active Directory and needs only basic features: user accounts, group membership, domain join, and Kerberos-based SSO. It does not need trusts, MFA, or schema extensions. Which option is MOST cost-effective?
options: AWS Managed Microsoft AD (Enterprise Edition)
AD Connector
Simple AD
Self-managed Active Directory on two EC2 instances
explanation: Simple AD is a low-scale, low-cost, Samba 4-based directory that supports basic Active Directory features, works with WorkSpaces, and provides LDAP for Linux workloads, which fits a small company without advanced requirements. AWS Managed Microsoft AD Enterprise Edition is sized for very large directories and costs more. AD Connector requires an existing on-premises directory, and self-managed domain controllers add instance and administration costs.

question: A solutions architect is documenting the availability characteristics of a new AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory for a disaster recovery review. Which statements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: By default, the directory runs two domain controllers that are deployed across two Availability Zones.
The domain controllers can be assigned Elastic IP addresses so that clients on the internet can authenticate directly.
The company must install monitoring agents on each domain controller so that AWS can detect failures.
Failed domain controllers are replaced automatically, and AWS takes a backup of the directory once per day.
The directory runs a single domain controller until additional domain controllers are deployed manually.
explanation: AWS Managed Microsoft AD provisions two domain controllers in two Availability Zones for fault tolerance, automatically replaces failed domain controllers in the same AZ with the same IP address, and takes daily backups. Elastic IP addresses cannot be attached to the directory's network interfaces, and AWS does not allow monitoring agents to be installed on the domain controllers. Additional domain controllers are optional for more resiliency and performance, not required to get past a single one.

question: A company runs a steady baseline of Amazon Aurora, Amazon RDS for Oracle, and Amazon DynamoDB usage. Over the next year it plans to migrate RDS for Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition and to move some workloads between Regions. The company wants a commitment-based discount that keeps applying through these changes. Which purchase option meets these requirements?
options: Reserved DB instances for the current RDS for Oracle instance class in the current Region
Database Savings Plans sized to the steady hourly database spend
Compute Savings Plans sized to the steady hourly database spend
EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the instance family that the databases use
explanation: Database Savings Plans apply to Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, and other database services regardless of engine, instance family, size, or Region, so the discount follows a move from RDS for Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL. Reserved DB instances must match the Region, DB engine, and instance type, so an engine migration ends the discount. Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate, and Lambda, and EC2 Instance Savings Plans cover EC2 instances only, not managed database usage.

question: A company runs a stable fleet of M-family EC2 instances in eu-west-1 that will run 24/7 for at least 3 years. It expects to change instance sizes and move some instances from Windows to Linux, but it will not change the instance family or Region, and it does not use AWS Fargate or AWS Lambda. Which option provides the LARGEST discount for this usage?
options: A 3-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the M family in eu-west-1
A 3-year Compute Savings Plan sized to the fleet's hourly spend
Spot Instances requested through an EC2 Fleet with a capacity-optimized strategy
On-Demand Capacity Reservations for the fleet in each Availability Zone
explanation: EC2 Instance Savings Plans offer up to 72 percent off On-Demand in exchange for committing to an instance family in a Region, and they still apply across sizes, operating systems, and tenancy within that family, which matches the planned changes. Compute Savings Plans offer up to 66 percent because they add flexibility across families, Regions, Fargate, and Lambda that this company does not need. Spot Instances can be interrupted, and Capacity Reservations are billed at On-Demand rates.

question: A company opted in to AWS Compute Optimizer. Its Java application servers on EC2 are memory-bound, but Compute Optimizer recommends instance types based only on CPU, network, and disk metrics, and some recommended types would run out of memory. How can the company get rightsizing recommendations that account for memory usage?
options: Enable detailed monitoring on the instances so that memory metrics are published every minute.
Enable the AWS Trusted Advisor low utilization check so that Compute Optimizer imports memory data.
Create a Cost Explorer rightsizing report filtered on the memory-optimized instance families that the application servers use.
Install the CloudWatch agent on the instances to publish memory utilization with the InstanceId dimension.
explanation: Compute Optimizer analyzes memory utilization only when the CloudWatch agent publishes it (for example, mem_used_percent in the CWAgent namespace with the InstanceId dimension), or when memory metrics are ingested from a supported observability product. Detailed monitoring increases the frequency of hypervisor-level metrics but does not add memory metrics. Trusted Advisor and Cost Explorer reports do not feed memory data into Compute Optimizer.

question: A company with 40 accounts in AWS Organizations wants rightsizing recommendations for its EC2 instances, EBS volumes, and Lambda functions in every account, viewed from one place. Several workloads have month-end processing peaks, and recommendations must not undersize resources for those peaks. Which actions should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)
options: Enable AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitors for each linked account to flag oversized resources.
Opt in to AWS Compute Optimizer from the management account for all member accounts.
Create AWS Budgets usage budgets for EC2, EBS, and Lambda in each account with alerts at 80 percent of expected usage.
Enable S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics for the organization to extend the metrics lookback period.
Activate the Compute Optimizer enhanced infrastructure metrics preference to extend the lookback period to 93 days.
explanation: Compute Optimizer generates recommendations for EC2 instances, EBS volumes, Lambda functions, and other resources, and opting in from the management account lets the team view findings across member accounts. By default it analyzes 14 days of metrics, so enhanced infrastructure metrics, which extend the lookback to 93 days, capture monthly peaks. Cost Anomaly Detection and Budgets track spend and usage rather than resource sizing, and Storage Lens analyzes S3 storage.

question: A company with the AWS Basic Support plan opens the AWS Trusted Advisor console and sees all Service Limits checks and a few security and fault tolerance checks, but no cost optimization checks such as low-utilization EC2 instances or idle load balancers. What must the company do to use these checks?
options: Enable Trusted Advisor in every AWS Region where resources run so that it can collect the utilization data that cost checks need.
Enable AWS Config recording in each Region so that Trusted Advisor can evaluate resource utilization for the cost checks.
Upgrade to a support plan that includes the full set of Trusted Advisor checks, such as Enterprise Support.
Opt in to AWS Cost Explorer from the management account so that its usage data is shared with Trusted Advisor.
explanation: With Basic Support, Trusted Advisor provides all Service Limits checks and selected security and fault tolerance checks; the full set of checks, including cost optimization, requires a higher support plan such as Business Support+, Enterprise Support, or Unified Operations. Trusted Advisor is not enabled per Region, and enabling AWS Config or Cost Explorer does not unlock additional Trusted Advisor checks.

question: A finance team wants to be alerted when spending on any AWS service or in any linked account rises unusually compared with its normal pattern, without having to choose fixed dollar thresholds, and wants to see the likely root cause of each spike. Which AWS feature meets these requirements?
options: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection with monitors and alert subscriptions
AWS Budgets cost budgets with forecasted-spend alerts for each service
A CloudWatch alarm on the EstimatedCharges metric for each linked account
AWS Cost Explorer saved reports grouped by service and linked account
explanation: Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to learn spend patterns, including seasonality and growth, sends alerts by email or Amazon SNS, and ranks root causes by service, account, Region, and usage type. Budgets and billing alarms rely on fixed thresholds that must be chosen and maintained. Cost Explorer reports are for analysis and do not send anomaly alerts.

question: A company purchased Compute Savings Plans last quarter. The FinOps team must be notified on any day that less than 90 percent of the purchased commitment is used, and on any day that less than 70 percent of eligible compute usage is covered by Savings Plans. Which budgets should the team create in AWS Budgets? (Select TWO.)
options: A cost budget with a forecasted-spend alert at 90 percent of the monthly amount
A daily Savings Plans utilization budget with a 90 percent threshold
A daily Savings Plans coverage budget with a 70 percent threshold
A usage budget that tracks EC2 instance hours against a fixed limit
An RI coverage budget with a 70 percent threshold
